text: The hypothesis function h(x) must always produce values within the range of the training data's y values.

The hypothesis h(x) = θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ + ... is a linear function that can produce any real-valued output. It is not constrained to the range of training y values and can extrapolate beyond them based on the learned parameters θ.
Setting x₀ = 1 adds an extra feature to the dataset that must be measured or collected.

Setting x₀ = 1 is a notational convention to represent the intercept term θ₀ in vector form. It allows us to write h(x) = θᵀx compactly, where both θ and x are vectors. This is not a real feature but a mathematical trick for convenience.
The factor of 1/2 in the cost function J(θ) = (1/2)Σ(h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) - y⁽ⁱ⁾)² is necessary for the cost function to work correctly.

The factor of 1/2 is included for mathematical convenience. When we take the derivative of the squared term during gradient descent, the 2 from the power rule cancels with the 1/2, simplifying the calculations. The optimization result is the same whether we use 1/2 or not.
The cost function J(θ) measures the error on a single training example at a time.

The cost function J(θ) = (1/2)Σⁿᵢ₌₁(h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) - y⁽ⁱ⁾)² aggregates the squared errors across all n training examples. It provides a single scalar value representing how well the hypothesis fits the entire training set.
In gradient descent, we should update θ₀ first, then θ₁, then θ₂, and so on in sequence.

The gradient descent update θⱼ := θⱼ - α(∂/∂θⱼ)J(θ) must be performed simultaneously for all values of j. This means computing all partial derivatives using the current θ values, then updating all parameters at once, not sequentially.
A larger learning rate α always makes gradient descent converge faster to the optimal solution.

If the learning rate α is too large, gradient descent may overshoot the minimum, fail to converge, or even diverge. The learning rate must be chosen carefully to ensure convergence—smaller values are safer but slower, while larger values may be faster but risk instability.
The LMS update rule increases θⱼ when the prediction h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) is greater than the actual value y⁽ⁱ⁾.

The LMS update rule θⱼ := θⱼ + α(y⁽ⁱ⁾ - h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))xⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ actually decreases θⱼ when h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) > y⁽ⁱ⁾ and xⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ is positive, because the error term (y⁽ⁱ⁾ - h(x⁽ⁱ⁾)) becomes negative. The update moves parameters in the direction that reduces the error.
Batch gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent will always converge to the exact same parameter values.

Batch gradient descent converges to the global minimum for linear regression. Stochastic gradient descent oscillates around the minimum and may never converge to a fixed point, though it gets close. However, both methods find good approximations, and stochastic gradient descent is often preferred for large datasets due to faster initial progress.
Stochastic gradient descent updates parameters after looking at all training examples, just like batch gradient descent, but with a different formula.

Stochastic gradient descent updates parameters after each individual training example, using θⱼ := θⱼ + α(y⁽ⁱ⁾ - h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))xⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾. In contrast, batch gradient descent sums the gradients over all training examples before making a single update. This makes stochastic gradient descent faster to start making progress.
Gradient descent can get stuck in local minima when optimizing the linear regression cost function, so the solution depends on initialization.

The linear regression cost function J(θ) is a convex quadratic function with only one global minimum and no local minima. Therefore, gradient descent always converges to the same global optimum regardless of initialization, assuming the learning rate is not too large.
The normal equation and gradient descent will give different optimal parameters θ* for the same dataset.

Both the normal equation θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy and gradient descent (when properly converged) find the same optimal parameters that minimize J(θ). The normal equation solves for θ analytically in one step, while gradient descent finds it iteratively.
The normal equation is always better than gradient descent because it finds the exact solution immediately without iteration.

The normal equation requires computing (XᵀX)⁻¹, which has computational complexity around O(d³) where d is the number of features. For large d, this becomes prohibitively expensive, making gradient descent more practical despite requiring iteration.
Linear regression can only work with one or two features because the hypothesis function is a line or plane.

Linear regression works with any number of features. The hypothesis h(x) = Σᵈᵢ₌₀ θᵢxᵢ is linear in the parameters θ and can handle d-dimensional input spaces. The term 'linear' refers to the relationship being linear in parameters, not to the number of dimensions.
The probabilistic interpretation shows that linear regression only works when the errors are actually Gaussian distributed.

The Gaussian noise assumption provides one justification for least squares as maximum likelihood estimation, but it is not necessary for linear regression to be useful. Least-squares can be justified under other assumptions and remains a reasonable and effective procedure even when errors are not Gaussian.
Underfitting occurs when the model is too complex and memorizes the training data.

Underfitting occurs when the model is too simple to capture the underlying structure in the data. For example, fitting a linear function to data with clear nonlinear patterns results in underfitting. The model fails to represent the complexity present in the data.
A model that perfectly fits all training data points with zero error is always the best model.

A model that passes through every training point exactly may be overfitting. For example, a 5th-order polynomial that perfectly fits housing price data likely captures noise rather than true patterns, and will generalize poorly to new examples. Good models balance fit to training data with generalization ability.
Adding more features always improves model performance because it gives the model more information to work with.

While more features can improve fit on training data, adding too many features risks overfitting. A model with excessive features may fit training data perfectly but fail to generalize. Feature selection is important—models need enough features to capture true patterns but not so many that they fit noise.
Locally weighted linear regression is called 'locally weighted' because it assigns different weights to different features based on their importance.

Locally weighted linear regression assigns weights to training examples, not features. Training examples close to the query point x receive high weights w⁽ⁱ⁾ ≈ 1, while distant examples receive low weights. The term 'local' refers to giving more importance to nearby training data when making predictions.
Parametric algorithms like standard linear regression need to keep the entire training set in memory to make predictions.

Parametric algorithms like standard linear regression have a fixed number of parameters θ. Once these are learned from training data, we only need to store the parameter values to make predictions—the training data can be discarded. Non-parametric algorithms like locally weighted linear regression require keeping the entire training set.
The choice of features doesn't matter much as long as we have enough training data for the model to learn from.

Feature selection is critical to ensuring good performance. Poor feature choices can lead to underfitting if important patterns cannot be captured, or overfitting if too many irrelevant features are included. The notes emphasize that choosing appropriate features is an important design decision in learning problems.
The hypothesis function h(x) = θᵀx can only model linear relationships because it's called linear regression.

Linear regression can model nonlinear relationships through feature engineering. By including polynomial features like x², we can fit curves as shown with y = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x². The 'linear' refers to linearity in the parameters θ, not the features. The model remains linear in θ even with nonlinear feature transformations.
Minimizing the sum of absolute errors |h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) - y⁽ⁱ⁾| would give the same result as minimizing the sum of squared errors.

Squared errors and absolute errors lead to different optimal solutions. The least-squares cost function J(θ) = (1/2)Σ(h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) - y⁽ⁱ⁾)² is specifically chosen and corresponds to maximum likelihood estimation under Gaussian noise assumptions. Absolute errors would give a different optimization problem with different properties.
The gradient ∂J(θ)/∂θⱼ tells us the value we should set θⱼ to in order to minimize the cost function.

The gradient ∂J(θ)/∂θⱼ indicates the direction and rate of steepest increase of J. In gradient descent, we move in the opposite direction (θⱼ := θⱼ - α·∂J/∂θⱼ) to decrease J. The gradient does not directly give the optimal value; it guides iterative steps toward the minimum.
The variance σ² of the Gaussian noise must be known beforehand to perform linear regression using maximum likelihood.

The optimal θ obtained from maximizing the likelihood does not depend on the value of σ². Maximizing the log likelihood simplifies to minimizing the sum of squared errors, which is independent of σ². Therefore, we arrive at the same result even if σ² is unknown.
Logistic regression predicts continuous numerical values in the same way as linear regression.
Logistic regression is used for classification, where the target variable takes on discrete values, such as 0 or 1 in the binary case.
The labels 0 and 1 in binary classification are arbitrary numbers without meaning.
In binary classification, 0 represents the negative class and 1 represents the positive class.
Logistic regression directly uses θᵀx as its prediction.
In logistic regression, the hypothesis is defined as hθ(x) = g(θᵀx), where g is the sigmoid function.
The sigmoid function can produce values outside the range [0,1].
The sigmoid function always outputs values strictly between 0 and 1.
The derivative formula g′(z) = g(z)(1 − g(z)) applies to any increasing function.
The identity g′(z) = g(z)(1 − g(z)) is a specific property of the sigmoid function.
Logistic regression does not make probabilistic assumptions about the labels.
Logistic regression models the probability of each class label given the input features.
The likelihood expression works even if the training examples are not independent.
The likelihood formulation assumes that the training examples are generated independently.
Training logistic regression means minimizing the log-likelihood.
Logistic regression is trained by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data.
Logistic regression uses gradient descent with the same objective as linear regression.
Logistic regression uses gradient ascent because the objective is to maximize the log-likelihood.
Because the update rule looks the same, logistic regression and linear regression are the same algorithm.
Although the update rules have a similar form, logistic regression uses a nonlinear hypothesis function.
The logistic loss is unrelated to the likelihood of the model.
The logistic loss corresponds to the negative log-likelihood of the model.
Replacing the sigmoid with a threshold function preserves the probabilistic interpretation.
Using a threshold function yields the perceptron algorithm, which lacks a probabilistic interpretation.
In multiclass classification, the raw scores θᵢᵀx can be treated directly as probabilities.
The softmax function is used to convert raw scores into valid probabilities that sum to one.
The indicator function in the cross-entropy gradient represents a probability.
The indicator function equals 1 when the class label matches and 0 otherwise.
Newton’s method for logistic regression only uses first-order derivatives.
Newton’s method uses both the gradient and the Hessian of the objective function.
Discriminative models like logistic regression learn p(y|x) by first modeling p(x|y) and p(y), then applying Bayes rule.
Discriminative algorithms like logistic regression directly learn p(y|x) by modeling the decision boundary. Generative algorithms model p(x|y) and p(y), then use Bayes rule to derive p(y|x).
In Bayes rule, p(x) in the denominator represents the prior probability of the features.
In Bayes rule p(y|x) = p(x|y)p(y)/p(x), the term p(x) is the marginal probability of x, which serves as a normalization constant. The prior probability is p(y), not p(x).
In GDA, each class y=0 and y=1 must have different covariance matrices Σ₀ and Σ₁ to properly model the data.
In GDA, both classes share the same covariance matrix Σ. The model assumes p(x|y=0) ~ N(μ₀, Σ) and p(x|y=1) ~ N(μ₁, Σ), where only the means differ between classes.
The maximum likelihood estimate for μ₀ in GDA is computed by averaging all training examples, regardless of their labels.
The maximum likelihood estimate for μ₀ is the average of only those training examples where y⁽ⁱ⁾=0. Similarly, μ₁ is the average of examples where y⁽ⁱ⁾=1.
GDA and logistic regression always produce identical decision boundaries when applied to the same dataset.

GDA makes stronger modeling assumptions (Gaussian distribution) than logistic regression. When these assumptions are correct, GDA is more efficient and may perform better, but when they are incorrect, logistic regression is more robust.
The covariance matrix Σ in a multivariate normal distribution must be diagonal to ensure features are independent.
The covariance matrix Σ captures correlations between features. When Σ is diagonal, features are uncorrelated, but Σ need not be diagonal in general—it can model dependencies between features.
The Naive Bayes assumption states that all features xᵢ are independent of each other without any conditioning.
The Naive Bayes assumption states that features xᵢ are conditionally independent given the class label y. This means p(x|y) = ∏ p(xᵢ|y), where independence is assumed only after conditioning on y.
In text classification with Naive Bayes, the parameter φₖ|y=1 represents the probability that word k appears exactly once in emails that are spam.
The parameter φₖ|y=1 = p(xₖ=1|y=1) represents the probability that word k appears at least once in an email given that the email is spam, not the probability of appearing exactly once.
Laplace smoothing is only necessary when the training set is very small, and can be safely ignored for large datasets.

Laplace smoothing is necessary whenever there's a risk that some feature value never appears with a particular class label in the training data, which would cause p(x|y)=0 and make predictions impossible. This can occur even in moderately large datasets.
With Laplace smoothing, the formula φⱼ = (∑I{zⱼ=1} + 1)/(m + 2) adds 1 to the numerator and 2 to the denominator because there are always exactly 2 possible classes.

The formula φⱼ = (∑I{zⱼ=1} + 1)/(m + k) adds 1 to the numerator and k to the denominator, where k is the number of possible values the variable can take. For binary variables k=2, but for multinomial variables k could be different.
The multi-variate Bernoulli event model and multinomial event model will always produce the same classification results for text data.

The multi-variate Bernoulli and multinomial event models make different assumptions and typically produce different results. The Bernoulli model only tracks presence/absence of words, while the multinomial model accounts for word frequency and email length.
In the multinomial event model, each email generates exactly n words where n is fixed across all documents.

In the multinomial event model, email length n is determined by a Poisson(ξ) distribution, so different emails can have different lengths. The model then generates n words independently according to the multinomial distribution.
To classify a new example using Naive Bayes, we should pick the class y that maximizes p(x|y).

To classify a new example, we pick the class y that maximizes p(y|x), which by Bayes rule is proportional to p(x|y)p(y). We must account for both the likelihood and the prior probability of each class.
Generative models are always superior to discriminative models because they model the full joint distribution p(x,y).

Generative models make stronger assumptions about the data distribution. When these assumptions hold, they can be more data-efficient, but when assumptions are violated, discriminative models that directly learn p(y|x) are often more robust.
The parameter φ in GDA represents the mean of the Gaussian distribution for class y=1.
The parameter φ in GDA represents the prior probability p(y=1), not the mean. The means of the Gaussian distributions are denoted by μ₀ and μ₁ for the two classes.
In the multinomial event model for text classification, the likelihood p(x|y) depends on the order in which words appear in the email.

The multinomial event model treats the email as a bag of words, ignoring word order. The likelihood is p(x|y) = ∏ᵢ p(xᵢ|y), which depends only on which words appear and their frequencies, not their positions.
Generalized Linear Models are a completely different type of model unrelated to linear or logistic regression.
Linear regression and logistic regression are both special cases of the Generalized Linear Model framework.
Any probability distribution can be written in exponential family form.
Only distributions that can be written in the form p(y;η) = b(y)exp(ηᵀT(y) − a(η)) belong to the exponential family.
The natural parameter η is always equal to the mean of the distribution.
The natural parameter η is a parameter of the exponential family distribution and is not always equal to the mean.
The sufficient statistic T(y) must always be a complex function of y.
In many examples considered, including Bernoulli and Gaussian distributions, the sufficient statistic is simply T(y) = y.
The log partition function a(η) has no effect on the probability distribution.
The log partition function ensures the distribution is properly normalized so that probabilities sum or integrate to one.
Only Bernoulli distributions belong to the exponential family.
The exponential family includes many distributions such as Bernoulli, Gaussian, multinomial, Poisson, and others.
Generalized Linear Models are defined without any assumptions about the data-generating process.
GLMs are constructed by making specific assumptions about the conditional distribution of y given x.
In a GLM, the hypothesis function is chosen arbitrarily.
In a GLM, the hypothesis is chosen so that it predicts the expected value of T(y) given x.
The relationship between the natural parameter η and x must always be nonlinear.
In the GLM framework presented, the natural parameter η is assumed to be a linear function of x.
Ordinary least squares cannot be derived from the GLM framework.
Ordinary least squares arises as a GLM when the conditional distribution of y given x is modeled as Gaussian.
In the Gaussian GLM example, the hypothesis does not depend on the natural parameter.
For the Gaussian distribution in the GLM framework, the mean equals the natural parameter, which equals θᵀx.
Logistic regression does not fit into the Generalized Linear Model framework.
Logistic regression is a GLM obtained by modeling y|x with a Bernoulli distribution.
The logistic function is chosen arbitrarily in logistic regression.
The logistic function arises naturally as the mean of the Bernoulli distribution in the GLM formulation.
The canonical response function always equals the identity function.
The canonical response function depends on the distribution; it is the identity for Gaussian and the logistic function for Bernoulli.
The canonical link function maps inputs x directly to predictions.
The canonical link function is the inverse of the canonical response function and maps the mean to the natural parameter.
